etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French paradoxe, from Latin paradoxum, from Ancient Greek παράδοξος (parádoxos, “unexpected, strange”).

definitions.definition: An apparently self-contradictory statement, which can only be true if it is false, and vice versa.

quote.citation: 1909, William James, A pluralistic universe. Hibbert lectures, page 347:
quote.text: The active sense of living which we all enjoy, before reflection shatters our instinctive world for us, is self-luminous and suggests no paradoxes.

quote.citation: 1962, Abraham Wolf, Textbook of Logic‎[1], page 255:
quote.text: According to one version of an ancient paradox, an Athenian is supposed to say "I am a liar." It is then argued that if the statement is true, then he is telling the truth, and is therefore not a liar  […]

quote.citation: 1983 May 21, Ronald Reagan, Presidential Radio Address:
quote.text: The most fundamental paradox is that if we're never to use force, we must be prepared to use it and to use it successfully.

definitions.definition: A claim that two apparently contradictory ideas are true.

quote.citation: 1879, W. S. Gilbert, “The Pirates of Penzance”, in The Complete Plays of Gilbert and Sullivan, published 1941:
quote.text: How quaint the ways of Paradox! / At common sense she gaily mocks! / Though counting in the usual way years twenty-one I've been alive, / Yet reck'ning by my natal day, / Yet reck'ning by my natal day, / I am a little boy of five!

definitions.definition: A thing involving contradictory yet interrelated elements that exist simultaneously and persist over time.[1][2]
A person or thing having contradictory properties.

quote.citation: 1999, Virginia Henley, A Year and a Day‎[2], →ISBN, page 315:
quote.text: You are a paradox of bitch and angel.

definitions.definition: An unanswerable question or difficult puzzle, particularly one which leads to a deeper truth.

quote.citation: 1994, James Joseph Pirkl, Transgenerational Design‎[3], →ISBN, page 3:
quote.text: And only by dismantling our preconceptions of age can we be free to understand the paradox: How young are the old?

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A statement which is difficult to believe, or which goes against general belief.

quote.citation: 1594, William Shakespeare, The Tragedy of Hamlet, Prince of Denmark, Act III:
quote.text: Ay, truly; for the power of beauty will sooner / transform honesty from what it is to a bawd than the / force of honesty can translate beauty into his / likeness: this was sometime a paradox, but now the / time gives it proof.

quote.citation: 1615, Ralph Hamor, A True Discourse of the Present State of Virginia, Richmond, published 1957, page 3:
quote.text: they contended to make that Maxim, that there is no faith to be held with Infidels, a meere and absurd Paradox [...].

definitions.definition: (uncountable) The use of counterintuitive or contradictory statements (paradoxes) in speech or writing.

quote.citation: 1906, Richard Holt Hutton, Brief Literary Criticisms‎[4], page 40:
quote.text: The need for paradox is no doubt rooted deep in the very nature of the use we make of language.

definitions.definition: (uncountable, philosophy) A state in which one is logically compelled to contradict oneself.

quote.citation: 1866, Edward Poste, Aristotle on Fallacies, Or, The Sophistici Elenchi‎[5], translation of original by Aristotle, page 43:
quote.text: Thus, like modern disputants, they aimed either to confute the respondent or to land him in paradox.

definitions.definition: (countable, uncountable, psychotherapy) The practice of giving instructions that are opposed to the therapist's actual intent, with the intention that the client will disobey or be unable to obey.

quote.citation: 1988, Martin Lakin, Ethical Issues in the Psychotherapies‎[6], →ISBN, page 103:
quote.text: Defiance-based paradox is employed so that the family will actively oppose and deliberately sabotage the prescription.
